```{r}
#| label: setup - load libraries, data and create covariates in models table
#| include: false
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Display with kable for nice formatting
library(knitr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tinytex)
library(quarto)
library(lubridate)
library(flextable)
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(reactable)
library(leaflet)
library(leaflet.extras)
library(kableExtra)
library(gt)
library(RColorBrewer)


# Ensure proper initialization order
options(htmlwidgets.TOJSON_ARGS = list(na = 'string'))

#load sampling effort csv
samplingE <- read.csv("Data/Analyzed/SummarySamplingEffort.csv")
parksSamplingE <- read.csv("Data/Analyzed/ParksSamplingEffort.csv")
#remove extra column with numebrs
samplingE$X <- NULL
parksSamplingE$X <- NULL

#get the number of grids sampled in 2025
SampledGrids2025 <- samplingE$`Number of Grids`[samplingE$Year==2025]

# Species excluded from stationary reporting due to insufficient precision or data
excluded_stationary <- c("PAHE", "TABR")
excluded_transect <- c("EUMA","LABO","MYSE","MYTH","COTO","MYCI")
excluded_regional <- c("PAHE", "TABR")

# Load the model covariates summary table
model_covariates <- read.csv("Data/Analyzed/ActivityTrends/ModelVariables.csv")
transect_covariates <- read.csv("Data/Analyzed/ActivityTrends/ModelVariables_Transect.csv")
#this comes from running the ModelSelection.R code where it runs all of the covariates and chooses the best model best on AIC

#upload summary data for map
site_list <- readRDS("Data/Analyzed/MapDataSummary.rds")

#format the covariates df 
# Species code to common name lookup
species_names <- c(
  ANPA = "Pallid Bat",
  COTO = "Townsend's Big-eared Bat",
  EPFU = "Big Brown Bat",
  EUMA = "Spotted Bat",
  LABO = "Eastern Red Bat",
  LACI = "Hoary Bat",
  LANO = "Silver-haired Bat",
  MYLU = "Little Brown Myotis",
  MYYU = "Yuma Myotis",
  MYEV = "Long-eared Myotis",
  MYTH = "Fringed Myotis",
  MYVO = "Long-legged Myotis",
  MYCA = "California Myotis",
  MYCI = "Western Small-footed Myotis",
  PAHE = "Canyon Bat",
  TABR = "Mexican Free-tailed Bat",
  MYSE = "Northern Myotis"
)

# Clean covariate from models and format for report
model_covariates<- model_covariates %>%
  filter(!sp %in% excluded_stationary) %>%
  mutate(
    Common_Name = species_names[sp],
    Covariates = vars
  ) %>%
  select(Common_Name, Species_Code = sp, Covariates)

transect_covariates<- transect_covariates %>%
  filter(!sp %in% excluded_transect) %>%
  mutate(
    Common_Name = species_names[sp],
    Covariates = vars
  ) %>%
  select(Common_Name, Species_Code = sp, Covariates)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup - creating interactive map
#| include: false
#| cache: true
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

#specify when document is html vs pdf so that thing render as needed
is_html <- knitr::pandoc_to("html")
is_pdf <- !is_html

#Need to specify figure captions based on the rendering type (PDF or HTML)
cap_sitesummary <- paste0(
  "Acoustic bat monitoring sites in British Columbia, 2016–2025. Regions were defined by Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCSC) from species range maps to group areas with similar species composition.",
  if (is_html) paste0(
    "Click any site to view a summary of species detections by year. Summaries include manually verified detections and automated identifications where two auto-ID programs agreed on the species."
  ) else ""
)


# ── 1. Species cols ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
sp_cols <- c("ANPA","COTO","EPFU","EUMA","LABO","LACI","LANO",
             "MYCA","MYCI","MYEV","MYLU","MYSE","MYTH","MYVO","MYYU",
             "PAHE","TABR")

# ── 2. Colour palette ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
sp_colors <- c(
  "ANPA" = "#3A86FF", "COTO" = "#FB5607", "EPFU" = "#F28E2B",
  "EUMA" = "#FF006E", "LABO" = "#8338EC", "LACI" = "#06D6A0",
  "LANO" = "#E15759", "MYCA" = "#118AB2", "MYCI" = "#FFD166",
  "MYEV" = "#4E79A7", "MYLU" = "#59A14F", "MYSE" = "#F94144",
  "MYTH" = "#43AA8B", "MYVO" = "#9B59B6", "MYYU" = "#76B7B2",
  "PAHE" = "#EDC948", "TABR" = "#A05195", "Other" = "#AAAAAA"
)

# ── 3. SVG pie helper ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
make_pie_svg <- function(values, colors, size = 96) {
  total <- sum(values)
  if (total == 0) return(NULL)
  fracs  <- values / total
  angles <- cumsum(c(0, fracs)) * 2 * pi
  r <- size / 2 - 2
  slices <- purrr::map2_chr(seq_along(values), colors, function(i, col) {
    a0 <- angles[i]; a1 <- angles[i + 1]
    if (abs(a1 - a0) >= 2 * pi - 1e-6) {
      sprintf('<circle cx="%s" cy="%s" r="%s" fill="%s"/>',
              size/2, size/2, r, col)
    } else {
      x0 <- size/2 + r*sin(a0); y0 <- size/2 - r*cos(a0)
      x1 <- size/2 + r*sin(a1); y1 <- size/2 - r*cos(a1)
      large <- if ((a1 - a0) > pi) 1L else 0L
      sprintf('<path d="M %s %s L %s %s A %s %s 0 %s 1 %s %s Z" fill="%s" stroke="white" stroke-width="1"/>',
              size/2, size/2, x0, y0, r, r, large, x1, y1, col)
    }
  })
  svg <- sprintf('<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="%s" height="%s">%s</svg>',
                 size, size, paste(slices, collapse = ""))
  paste0("data:image/svg+xml;base64,", base64enc::base64encode(charToRaw(svg)))
}

# ── 4. HTML table body helper ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
make_sp_table <- function(sp_df, pie_colors) {
  sp_df %>%
    arrange(desc(n)) %>%
    mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1)) %>%
    purrr::pmap_chr(function(species, n, pct) sprintf(
      '<tr><td style="padding-right:8px"><span style="display:inline-block;width:10px;height:10px;border-radius:50%%;background:%s;margin-right:4px"></span>%s</td><td align="right" style="padding-right:6px">%s</td><td align="right">%s%%</td></tr>',
      ifelse(species %in% names(pie_colors), pie_colors[species], "#AAAAAA"),
      species, format(n, big.mark = ","), pct
    )) %>%
    paste(collapse = "")
}

# ── 5. Build popup HTML for each site ──────────────────────────────────────────
build_popup <- function(site_name, sp, years) {
  
  # Sites with no detections at all get NA (filtered out below)
  if (is.null(sp) || nrow(sp) == 0 || sum(sp$n, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) {
    return(NA_character_)
  }
  
  # -- One pie + species table per year (most recent first) ------------------
  year_blocks <- purrr::map_chr(sort(years, decreasing = TRUE), function(yr) {
    sp_yr <- sp %>%
      filter(year == yr) %>%
      group_by(species) %>%
      summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") %>%
      arrange(desc(n))
    
    if (nrow(sp_yr) == 0 || sum(sp_yr$n) == 0) return("")
    
    yr_total <- sum(sp_yr$n)
    
    # Colours: known palette + fallback for anything unmapped
    yr_species <- sp_yr$species
    unknown    <- setdiff(yr_species, names(sp_colors))
    fallback   <- setNames(
      colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(8, "Dark2"))(max(length(unknown), 1)),
      unknown)
    yr_colors  <- c(sp_colors, fallback)
    
    uri         <- make_pie_svg(sp_yr$n, yr_colors[yr_species], size = 96)
    legend_rows <- make_sp_table(sp_yr, yr_colors)
    
    sprintf(
      '<div style="margin-bottom:14px;">
         <div style="font-weight:600;font-size:13px;margin-bottom:6px;color:#333;">%s</div>
         <div style="display:flex;align-items:flex-start;gap:12px;">
           <img src="%s" width="96" height="96" style="flex-shrink:0;"/>
           <table style="font-size:11px;border-collapse:collapse;">
             <tr><th align="left" style="padding-right:8px">Species</th><th align="right" style="padding-right:6px">n</th><th align="right">%%</th></tr>
             %s
           </table>
         </div>
         <div style="font-weight:600;font-size:12px;margin-top:4px;color:#333;">Total bats: %s</div>
       </div>',
      yr, uri, legend_rows, format(yr_total, big.mark = ",")
    )
  }) %>% paste(collapse = "")
  
  # -- Popup: stacked yearly pies --------------------------------------------
  sprintf(
    '<div style="font-family:sans-serif;min-width:270px;max-width:340px;max-height:420px;overflow-y:auto;">
       <b style="font-size:14px;">%s</b>
       <hr style="margin:6px 0"/>
       %s
     </div>',
    site_name, year_blocks
  )
}

sites_plot <- site_list %>%
  mutate(popup = purrr::pmap_chr(
    list(site_name, sp_data, years),
    build_popup
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(popup))

# ── 5b. One searchable point per GRTS cell (centre of its sites) ───────────────
grts_search_pts <- sites_plot %>%
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%              # harmless if sites_plot isn't sf
  group_by(grts_id) %>%
  summarise(Long = mean(Long),
            Lat  = mean(Lat),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(grts_label = as.character(grts_id))

# ── 6. Load spatial data ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
transects_sf <- st_read("Data/Mapping/transects_merged.shp", quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_zm() |>                                   # drop any Z/M values Leaflet can't use
  st_transform(crs = 4326)
transects_sf <- transects_sf[!st_is_empty(transects_sf), ]

regions <- st_read("Data/Mapping/BC-SEAK Hub Regions Mar 2025.shp", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
  filter(Region != "AK") %>%
  mutate(Region_Merged = case_when(
    Region %in% c("HG", "WC", "NE", "NW") ~ "Northern",
    Region == "SE"                          ~ "Southeast",
    Region == "SC"                          ~ "Southcentral",
    Region == "SW"                          ~ "Southwest",
    TRUE                                    ~ Region
  )) %>%
  group_by(Region_Merged) %>%
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry)) %>%
  rename(Region = Region_Merged)

region_colors <- c(
  "Northern"     = "#70A800",
  "Southeast"    = "#E6E600",
  "Southcentral" = "#E64C00",
  "Southwest"    = "#0084A8"
)

pal_regions <- colorFactor(
  palette = unname(region_colors),
  levels  = names(region_colors)
)


# ── 7. Regions legend (custom HTML) ────────────────────────────────────────────
region_legend_html <- htmltools::tags$div(
  style = "background:white;padding:10px 14px;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.3);font-family:sans-serif;font-size:12px;",
  htmltools::tags$b("Analysis Regions"),
  htmltools::tags$hr(style = "margin:4px 0"),
  htmltools::HTML(paste(purrr::map_chr(names(region_colors), ~sprintf(
    '<div style="display:flex;align-items:center;margin-bottom:3px"><span style="display:inline-block;width:14px;height:14px;background:%s;opacity:0.6;border:1px solid gray;margin-right:6px"></span>%s</div>',
    region_colors[.x], .x)), collapse = ""))
)

# ── 8. Build the full map in one pipeline ──────────────────────────────────────
m_full <- leaflet() %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas) %>%
  
  # Custom panes: regions/transects sit BELOW circle markers (overlayPane = 400)
  addMapPane("regionsPane",   zIndex = 240) %>%
  addMapPane("transectsPane", zIndex = 260) %>%
  
  addPolygons(
    data        = regions,
    fillColor   = ~pal_regions(Region),
    fillOpacity = 0.2,
    color       = "gray",
    weight      = 2,
    label       = ~Region,
    group       = "Analysis Regions",
    options     = pathOptions(pane = "regionsPane")
  ) %>%
  
  addPolylines(
    data             = transects_sf,
    color            = "darkgreen",
    weight           = 3,
    opacity          = 0.7,
    label            = ~paste0("GRTS ID: ", GRTS_ID,
                               " | Years Sampled: ", N_Years,
                               " | Years: ", Yrs_Smp),
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(
      color        = "darkgreen",
      weight       = 5,
      bringToFront = TRUE
    ),
    group   = "Transects",
    options = pathOptions(pane = "transectsPane")
  ) %>%
  
  # All site markers in one vectorised call
  addCircleMarkers(
    data        = sites_plot,
    lng         = ~Long,
    lat         = ~Lat,
    radius      = 6,
    stroke      = TRUE,
    color       = "#ffffff",
    weight      = 1.5,
    fillColor   = "#3A86FF",
    fillOpacity = 0.9,
    popup       = ~popup,
    label       = ~site_name
  ) %>%
  # Invisible, non-clickable markers used only by the search bar
  addCircleMarkers(
    data        = grts_search_pts,
    lng         = ~Long,
    lat         = ~Lat,
    radius      = 1,
    opacity     = 0,
    fillOpacity = 0,
    label       = ~grts_label,
    group       = "grts_search",
    options     = pathOptions(interactive = FALSE)  # won't block clicks on real sites
  ) %>%
  addSearchFeatures(
    targetGroups = "grts_search",
    options = searchFeaturesOptions(
      propertyName         = "label",
      textPlaceholder      = "Search GRTS ID…",
      zoom                 = 11,     # a 10 × 10 km GRTS cell fits well at 11–12
      initial              = FALSE,  # partial IDs still match
      openPopup            = FALSE,
      firstTipSubmit       = TRUE,
      autoCollapse         = TRUE,
      hideMarkerOnCollapse = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  addControl(region_legend_html, position = "bottomright") %>%
  addLayersControl(
    overlayGroups = c("Analysis Regions", "Transects"),
    options       = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  addScaleBar(position = "bottomleft")

m_full
```

```{r}
#| label: setup - trend results
#| include: false
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

bc.cov.slope.summary.singlet <- read.csv("Data/Analyzed/ActivityTrends/bc.cov.estimates.singlet.csv")
bc.cov.slope.transect <- read.csv("Data/Analyzed/ActivityTrends/bc.transect.cov.estimates.csv")


# Prepare stationary data
stationary <- bc.cov.slope.summary.singlet %>%
  filter(!SpeciesGroup %in% excluded_stationary) %>%
  select(SpeciesGroup, Estimate, SE, p.value) %>%
  mutate(
    trend_ci = sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", Estimate, 1.96 * SE),
    p_val = case_when(
      p.value < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
      TRUE ~ sprintf("%.3f", p.value)
    )
  ) %>%
  select(SpeciesGroup, trend_ci, p_val, p.value) %>%
  dplyr::rename(stationary_trend = trend_ci, stationary_p = p_val, stationary_pval = p.value)

# Prepare transect data
transect <- bc.cov.slope.transect %>%
  filter(!SpeciesGroup %in% excluded_transect) %>%
  mutate(
    p_raw     = trimws(p.value),
    p_numeric = as.numeric(sub(".*?([0-9]*\\.[0-9]+).*", "\\1", p_raw)),
    trend_ci  = sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", Estimate, 1.96 * SE),
    p_val = case_when(
      grepl("<", p_raw)  ~ "<0.001",
      is.na(p_numeric)   ~ NA_character_,
      p_numeric < 0.001  ~ "<0.001",
      TRUE               ~ sprintf("%.3f", p_numeric)
    )
  ) %>%
  select(SpeciesGroup, trend_ci, p_val, p_numeric) %>%
  rename(transect_trend = trend_ci, transect_p = p_val, transect_pval = p_numeric)

# Merge datasets
merged_table <- full_join(stationary, transect, by = "SpeciesGroup")
merged_table <- merged_table %>%
  mutate(Species = species_names[SpeciesGroup]) %>%
  mutate(
    stationary_trend = ifelse(SpeciesGroup %in% excluded_stationary, "", stationary_trend),
    stationary_p = ifelse(SpeciesGroup %in% excluded_stationary, "", stationary_p),
    stationary_pval = ifelse(SpeciesGroup %in% excluded_stationary, NA, stationary_pval)
  ) %>%
  select(Species, stationary_trend, stationary_p, stationary_pval,
         transect_trend, transect_p, transect_pval)

# Add excluded species back as empty rows so they still appear in the table
excluded_rows <- tibble(
  SpeciesCode = excluded_stationary,
  Species = species_names[excluded_stationary],
  stationary_trend = "",
  stationary_p = "",
  stationary_pval = NA_real_,
  transect_trend = "",
  transect_p = "",
  transect_pval = NA_real_
)

# Bind and sort alphabetically by species code
merged_table <- merged_table %>%
  mutate(SpeciesCode = names(species_names)[match(Species, species_names)]) %>%
  bind_rows(excluded_rows) %>%
  arrange(SpeciesCode) %>%
  select(-SpeciesCode)

# Replace NA with empty strings for display columns only
merged_table <- merged_table %>%
  mutate(SpeciesCode = names(species_names)[match(Species, species_names)]) %>%
  bind_rows(excluded_rows) %>%
  group_by(SpeciesCode) %>%
  arrange(
    desc(!is.na(stationary_pval) | stationary_trend != ""),
    desc(!is.na(transect_pval) | transect_trend != "")
  ) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(SpeciesCode) %>%
  select(-SpeciesCode) %>%
  mutate(
    stationary_trend = ifelse(is.na(stationary_trend), "", stationary_trend),
    stationary_p     = ifelse(is.na(stationary_p), "", stationary_p),
    transect_trend   = ifelse(is.na(transect_trend), "", transect_trend),
    transect_p       = ifelse(is.na(transect_p), "", transect_p)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: regional-models-prep
#| echo: false
#| warning: false  
#| message: false


region.cov.slope.summary.singlet <- read.csv("Data/Analyzed/ActivityTrends/region.slope.summary.singlet.csv")

# Species x region combinations excluded after model diagnostics
# (singular fit, < 20 non-zero cell-years, or dispersion ratio >= 2)
excluded_regional <- tribble(
  ~Region,                 ~SpeciesGroup,
  "Kootenay Region",       "LACI",   # singular fit
  "Northern Region",       "LACI",   # singular fit
  "Northern Region",       "MYVO",   # singular fit
  "Okanagan Region",       "ANPA",   # singular fit
  "Okanagan Region",       "MYVO",   # overdispersion (2.89)
  "South Coastal Region",  "EUMA",   # singular fit; 6 non-zero cell-years
  "South Coastal Region",  "LABO"    # singular fit; 9 non-zero cell-years
)

# Define desired species display order (adjust to match your table)
species_order <- c("ANPA", "COTO", "EPFU", "EUMA", "LABO", "LACI", "LANO",
                   "MYCA", "MYCI", "MYEV", "MYLU", "MYSE", "MYTH", "MYVO", "MYYU")

# Process regional data
regional_wide <- region.cov.slope.summary.singlet %>%
  anti_join(excluded_regional, by = c("Region", "SpeciesGroup")) %>%
  mutate(
    trend_ci = sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", Estimate, 1.96 * Std..Error),
    p_val = case_when(
      Pr...z.. < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
      TRUE ~ sprintf("%.3f", Pr...z..)
    ),
    is_sig = Pr...z.. < 0.05
  ) %>%
  select(Region, SpeciesGroup, trend_ci, p_val, is_sig) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Region,
    values_from = c(trend_ci, p_val, is_sig),
    names_glue = "{Region}_{.value}"
  )

regions <- c("Kootenay Region", "Northern Region", "Okanagan Region", "South Coastal Region")

# Build final display table
final_table <- tibble(SpeciesGroup = species_order) %>%
  left_join(regional_wide, by = "SpeciesGroup") %>%
  mutate(Species = species_names[SpeciesGroup])

# identify when html or latex for bolding
fmt <- ifelse(knitr::is_html_output(), "html", "latex")

# Apply bolding region by region
for (reg in regions) {
  trend_col <- paste0(reg, "_trend_ci")
  p_col     <- paste0(reg, "_p_val")
  sig_col   <- paste0(reg, "_is_sig")
  
  if (trend_col %in% names(final_table)) {
    sig <- !is.na(final_table[[sig_col]]) & final_table[[sig_col]]
    final_table[[trend_col]] <- ifelse(sig,
                                       cell_spec(final_table[[trend_col]], bold = TRUE, format = fmt),
                                       final_table[[trend_col]])
    final_table[[p_col]] <- ifelse(sig,
                                   cell_spec(final_table[[p_col]], bold = TRUE, format = fmt),
                                   final_table[[p_col]])
  }
}

# Drop is_sig columns and select final columns
final_table <- final_table %>%
  select(Species, all_of(paste0(rep(regions, each = 2), c("_trend_ci", "_p_val"))))

# Replace NA values with empty strings
final_table <- final_table %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace_na(as.character(.x), "")))

col_names <- c("Species", rep(c("Estimate ± 95%CI", "P-value"), length(regions)))
```

```{r}
#| label: setup - slider occupancy map

#site-year summary for interactive slider maps code
#this creates a map that can go between species and show the slider maps with P(occupancy for all the sites where the species was detected)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

old_tojson <- options(htmlwidgets.TOJSON_ARGS = NULL)

make_occ_species_map <- function(species,
                                 path   = "Data/Analyzed/OccupancyTables/") {                      # NEW
  pal_hex <- RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(9, "OrRd")
  pal_fun <- scales::col_numeric(pal_hex, domain = c(0, 1), na.color = "#bdbdbd")
  
  occ_all <- lapply(names(species), function(sp) {
    read.csv(file.path(path, paste0("site_year_occupancy_", sp, ".csv"))) |>
      mutate(sp_code = sp)
  }) |>
    bind_rows() |>
    mutate(
      surveyed   = as.logical(surveyed),
      detected   = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(detected)),
      p_occupied = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(p_occupied))
    ) |>
    filter(surveyed) |>
    mutate(
      status = ifelse(detected %in% 1, "Detected", "Not detected"),
      symbol = ifelse(status == "Detected", "circle", "triangle-up"),
      fill   = pal_fun(pmin(pmax(p_occupied, 0), 1)),
      hover  = paste0(
        "<b>", site, "</b><br>", region,
        "<br>Year: ", year,
        "<br>", status, " (", n_visits, " visits)",
        "<br>P(occupied): ", sprintf("%.2f", p_occupied),
        "<br>\u03c8 expected: ",
        sprintf("%.2f [%.2f\u2013%.2f]", psi_expected, psi_expected_lo95, psi_expected_hi95)
      )
    ) |>
    arrange(sp_code, year, site)
  
  # NEW: drop any species with no surveyed rows (avoids empty menu entries / min() of nothing)
  species <- species[names(species) %in% unique(occ_all$sp_code)]
  
  lon_rng <- range(occ_all$long, na.rm = TRUE) + c(-1, 1)
  lat_rng <- range(occ_all$lat,  na.rm = TRUE) + c(-0.5, 0.5)
  off_lat <- 0; off_lon <- 0
  
  p <- plot_ly() |>                                   
    add_trace(
      type = "scattergeo", mode = "markers",
      lat = off_lat, lon = off_lon, hoverinfo = "skip", showlegend = FALSE,
      marker = list(
        color = 0, cmin = 0, cmax = 1,
        colorscale = list(seq(0, 1, length.out = length(pal_hex)), pal_hex),
        showscale = TRUE,
        colorbar = list(title = list(text = "P(occupied)"), len = 0.45, y = 0.35,
                        tickvals = seq(0, 1, 0.25))
      )
    ) |>
    add_trace(type = "scattergeo", mode = "markers", lat = off_lat, lon = off_lon,
              name = "Detected", hoverinfo = "skip",
              marker = list(symbol = "circle", size = 11, color = "#bdbdbd",
                            line = list(color = "#4d4d4d", width = 1))) |>
    add_trace(type = "scattergeo", mode = "markers", lat = off_lat, lon = off_lon,
              name = "Not detected", hoverinfo = "skip",
              marker = list(symbol = "triangle-up", size = 11, color = "#bdbdbd",
                            line = list(color = "#4d4d4d", width = 1)))
  n_fixed <- 3
  
  key <- occ_all |> distinct(sp_code, year) |>
    filter(sp_code %in% names(species)) |>
    mutate(sp_code = factor(sp_code, levels = names(species))) |>
    arrange(sp_code, year) |>
    mutate(sp_code = as.character(sp_code))
  
  first_sp <- names(species)[1]
  first_yr <- min(key$year[key$sp_code == first_sp])
  
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(key))) {
    sub <- occ_all |> filter(sp_code == key$sp_code[i], year == key$year[i])
    p <- p |> add_trace(
      type = "scattergeo", mode = "markers",
      lat = sub$lat, lon = sub$long,
      text = sub$hover, hoverinfo = "text",
      name = paste(key$sp_code[i], key$year[i]), showlegend = FALSE,
      visible = key$sp_code[i] == first_sp & key$year[i] == first_yr,
      marker = list(symbol = sub$symbol, color = sub$fill, size = 12, opacity = 0.95,
                    line = list(color = "#4d4d4d", width = 1))
    )
  }
  
  vis <- function(sp, yr) as.list(c(rep(TRUE, n_fixed),
                                    key$sp_code == sp & key$year == yr))
  
  slider_for <- function(sp) {
    yrs <- key$year[key$sp_code == sp]
    list(list(
      active = 0,
      currentvalue = list(prefix = "Year: ", font = list(size = 16)),
      pad = list(t = 10),
      steps = lapply(yrs, function(y) list(
        label = as.character(y), method = "restyle",
        args = list("visible", vis(sp, y))
      ))
    ))
  }
  
  buttons <- lapply(names(species), function(sp) {
    y1 <- min(key$year[key$sp_code == sp])
    list(label = paste0(sp, " \u2013 ", species[[sp]]),             # NEW: code + common name
         method = "update",
         args = list(list(visible = vis(sp, y1)),
                     list(sliders = slider_for(sp))))
  })
  
  p |> layout(
    margin = list(t = 50, b = 80, l = 10, r = 10),                   # NEW: tighter margins
    updatemenus = list(list(
      type = "dropdown",                                             # NEW: dropdown, not buttons
      active = 0, showactive = TRUE,
      x = 0, xanchor = "left", y = 1.06, yanchor = "top",
      bgcolor = "white", bordercolor = "#9e9e9e",
      buttons = buttons
    )),
    sliders = slider_for(first_sp),
    geo = list(
      domain = list(x = c(0, 1), y = c(0, 1)),                       # NEW: map fills the plot area
      scope = "north america", resolution = 50,
      projection = list(type = "mercator"),
      showland = TRUE,  landcolor  = "#f7f7f7",
      showocean = TRUE, oceancolor = "#e8f0f5",
      showlakes = TRUE, lakecolor  = "#e8f0f5",
      showcountries = TRUE, countrycolor = "#9e9e9e",
      showsubunits  = TRUE, subunitcolor = "#c8c8c8",
      lonaxis = list(range = lon_rng),
      lataxis = list(range = lat_rng)
    ),
    legend = list(x = 1.02, y = 0.9)
  )
}
```

# Executive Summary

The North American Bat Monitoring (NABat) program is a multi-agency initiative administered by the US Geological Survey (USGS). In 2024, the North by Northwest (NNW) Bat Hub was formed by combining the former Alberta Hub and the BC and Southeast Alaska (BC-SE_AK) Hub. The NNW Bat Hub leads the NABat program within British Columbia, with key support from provincial and state representatives and WCSC.

In 2025, 57 grid cells throughout British Columbia were monitored. Two statistical analysis methods were used complimentary to evaluate the trends of bat species across the province. Results indicate that bat populations across British Columbia remain stable, with some key species showing small positive trends, including Little Brown Myotis and Eastern Red Bat. Given growing threats to bat populations in BC, continued monitoring is essential to detect any significant changes.

We acknowledge the traditional teachings of the lands that we work on, and that reciprocal, meaningful, and respectful relationships with Indigenous peoples make our work possible. {{< pagebreak >}}

# Introduction

## Overview of NABat and the NNW Bat Hub

North American Bat Monitoring Program (NABat) is a large-scale coordinated effort to monitor bat species to address gaps in knowledge and lack of long-term studies across North America [@loeb2015Plan].The program is administered by the US Geological Survey (USGS) and implemented by the North by Northwest Bat (NNW) Hub in British Columbia, Alberta and S.E Alaska.

NNW Bat Hub was established in 2024 with collaboration from Government of British Columbia, Government of Alberta, and Government of Alaska. The hub was formed by combining the previous Alberta Hub and the BC and southeast Alaska (BC-SE_AK) Hub. The implementation of the program within British Columbia has key support from Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCSC), government staff, other wildlife biologists, Indigenous Nations, community members and naturalists across the province.

The centralization of efforts for the hub will expand exciting programs to coordinate more efficiently across jurisdictions, ensuring consistent and long-term bat monitoring through standardized data collection, and streamlined bioacoustic data management. It also seeks to enhance engagement with NABat, foster collaboration among stakeholders, and produce annual reports on regional monitoring.

## Threats to bat populations in BC

Bat populations in British Columbia face a wide range of threats including forestry practices, anthropogenic expansion, and climate change among others. A comprehensive review of tese threats and their relative impacts on individual bat species can be found in the BC Bat Action Plan [@BCBatAction2024Plan]. Of these threats, White-Nose Syndrome and wind energy development have emerged as two of the highest-priority concerns.

### White-Nose Syndrome

White-nose Syndrome (WNS) is a deadly fungal disease caused by the fungus *Pseudogymnoascus destructans* (*Pd*) that affects hibernating bats. As of 2026, WNS has been confirmed in nine Canadian provinces including Alberta, and *Pd* has been detected within British Columbia at two locations ( @fig-WNS: @cwhc-rcsf2024Canadian). Continued monitoring of populations in BC is critical as *Pd* and WNS continue to spread throughout the province.

![White-nose syndrome (WNS) and Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd) occurrence in Canada. Source: CWHC-RCSF (2026)](Figures/20260226%20Pd%20Canada.png){#fig-WNS fig-pos="H"}

### Wind Energy Development

Wind energy farms has been linked to high mortality rates across all bat species in Canada, with long distance migratory species accounting for 73% of recorded fatalities [@zimmerling2016Bat]. In British Columbia alone, one estimate predicts an annual mortality rate of 680 bats per wind turbine [@zimmerling2016Bat]. There are currently close to 300 turbines active in the province across 10 different projects with the most turbines found in the Peace region (@fig-turbines). In late 2024, B.C announced nine new wind projects which would require the installation of over 300 new wind turbines across the province [@ministryofenergyandclimatesolutions2024BC]. As of 2023, COSEWIC designated all three of B.C.'s long distance migratory species as endangered due in part to fatalities at wind turbine facilities [@committeeonthestatusofendangeredwildlifeincanada2023Hoary].

![Current wind turbines in British Columbia based on the Canadian Wind Turbine Database (Source: https://search.open.canada.ca/openmap/79fdad93-9025-49ad-ba16-c26d718cc070)](Figures/WindTurbinesBC.JPG){#fig-turbines}

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Acoustic Monitoring of Bats

Acoustic recording is a cost-effective method for monitoring bat populations across large geographic and temporal scales. However, several limitations affect the conclusions that can be drawn from these data:

1.  **Imperfect species identification** --- Unlike birds, bats rely on echolocation rather than song, and species with similar ecology and physiology often produce overlapping calls. While detectors are deployed to maximize recordings of diagnostic Search Phase calls, species identifiability will always vary depending on the local assemblage.

2.  **Variable detectability** --- Bat species are not equally detectable acoustically. Larger, wide-ranging species produce louder calls that travel farther, while smaller species with quieter calls or specialized habitat use are less reliably recorded. As a result, trend estimates cannot be produced for all species using acoustic methods alone.

3.  **Data variability** --- Many factors influence recording quality and bat activity, including wind speed, humidity, and local habitat. Additionally, stationary detectors cannot account for individual recapture, meaning acoustic data can only inform relative activity and occupancy.

4.  **Processing limitations** --- Auto-ID software enables efficient processing of large datasets but has known high misclassification rates for bats, making manual verification necessary to ensure accurate results.

## Updates in Modelling Approaches

Bat monitoring data can be analyzed using different statistical approaches, each with distinct assumptions and outputs. Activity trend models examine changes in relative acoustic activity over time, providing a straightforward measure of whether bat detections are increasing, decreasing, or remaining stable across the monitoring network.

Dynamic occupancy models take a different approach, estimating the probability that a species occupies a given site while explicitly accounting for imperfect detection. Rather than treating a non-detection as an absence, these models distinguish between a species being truly absent and simply going undetected, an important consideration given the variable detectability of bats discussed above. They also track colonization and extinction probabilities across sites over time, providing insight into range shifts and local population dynamics.

The two approaches differ in sensitivity and therefore serve complementary roles. Activity data are inherently noisy, influenced by weather, local foraging conditions, and the number of individuals passing a detector, but they respond quickly to change and can provide an early indication of decline. Occupancy, in contrast, changes only when a species is lost from (or gains) sites, so a stronger and more sustained signal is needed before a trend becomes apparent. Occupancy models can therefore act as a second, more conservative test of patterns first suggested by activity data. When both approaches point in the same direction, the evidence for a real population change is stronger, and confidence in the results is correspondingly higher.

In 2025, both model types were run to examine differences in results and assess the complementary information each approach provides.

# Methods

## Data Collection

The BC NABat monitoring program was established in 2016 by Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCSC) and has since sampled 65 grid cells. Cells were drawn from the NABat Generalized Random Tessellation Stratified (GRTS) sampling frame [@loeb2015Plan], and selected based on accessibility, the presence of bat habitat, suitable recorder sites and in GRTS priority order. Where possible, cells were also selected based on the precense of a relatively straight road of 30–45 km for a driving transect.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: true
#| label: tbl-samp
#| tbl-cap: Total number active grid cells and number of site nights sampled summarized by calendar year in British Columbia. Site nights are defined as the cumulative number of nights during which recorders were operational
#| fig.pos: 'H'

kable(samplingE,
      col.names = c("Year", "Number of Grid Cells Sampled","Number of BC Parks Grids", "Site Nights"),
      label = "sampling-efforts",
      escape = FALSE,
      align = "ccc") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped"),
                full_width = FALSE,
                position = "center") %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "8em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "10em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "10em")%>%
  column_spec(4, width = "8em") 
  
```

In 2025 a total of `r samplingE[10,2]` grid cells were monitored for a total of `r samplingE[10,4]` site nights (@tbl-samp). Of the cells sampled in 2025 a total of `r samplingE[10,3]` were sampled by BC Parks staff (@tbl-samp-parks). The network is well-distributed across the province, with a slight bias toward southern BC and population centres (@fig-map).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: true
#| label: tbl-samp-parks
#| tbl-cap: Summary of yearly sampling of grid cells in BC Parks.
#| fig.pos: 'H'

kable(parksSamplingE,
      col.names = c("GRTS Cell ID", "Park", 2016:2025, "Total Years"),
      label = "parks-sampling",
      escape = FALSE,
      align = c("c", "l", rep("c", 10), "c")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped"),
                full_width = FALSE,
                position = "center") %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Year" = 10, " " = 1)) %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "6em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "10em") %>%
  column_spec(3:12, width = "3em") %>%
  column_spec(13, width = "6em")
```

### Stationary Surveys

Two to four stationary detectors were deployed across at least two quadrants per grid cell for a minimum of seven nights. Sites are selected to maximize species detection and recording quality across different habitat types (see @rae2024North for full site selection criteria). Deployment occured between mid-May and mid-July, after bats have emerged from hibernation but before young bats are volant. Sites and timing are kept consistent between years to minimize variability in conditions affecting bat activity.

### Transect Surveys

Where possible, driving transects were conducted following @loeb2015Plan. Two replicates of a 30--35 km route are driven at 30--35 km/h with a rooftop detector, using straight roads that minimize switchbacks. Transects are conducted concurrently with stationary deployments.

### Equipment

A wide range of equipment has been used across sampling locations in BC. Until 2024, stationary acoustic units were primarily Wildlife Acoustics SM4Bat-FS or SM2Bat units (Maynard, MA), alongside an increasing number of Titley Scientific Swift and Express units (Brisbane, AU). Mobile transects were conducted using either the Wildlife Acoustics EchoMeter Touch2Pro or Titley Scientific Anabat units (SD1/2 zero-cross or Walkabout models).

2025 represents a transition year for equipment standardization. All SM2Bat units are being replaced with Titley Scientific Chorus units, and Anabat units are being phased out in favour of the EchoMeter Touch2Pro for mobile transects. To account for detection differences between outgoing and incoming equipment, paired deployments were conducted at a number of grid cells this year, both stationary (SM2Bat and Chorus) and mobile (Anabat SD1 and EchoMeter Touch2Pro).

### Landscape and Weather Covariates

We used the same covariates for the activity trend models as @rae2022North. Where possible, temperature and relative humidity were recorded in each grid cell with onsite data loggers. Where loggers were unavailable, values came from the nearest climate station in the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium (PCIC) [Provincial Climate Data Set (PCDS)](https://www.uvic.ca/pcic/data-analysis-tools/data-portal/station-data/index.php), which aggregates and quality-controls observations from multiple provincial and federal networks. From these station records we also derived nightly mean wind speed (km/h) and nightly total precipitation (mm). Degree days above 10 °C since January 1 were calculated from daily temperature records for each site-night.

Sun and moon positions were calculated with the astral package (v3.2) in Python. Sunset and sunrise times defined the night period for each site-night. Moon illumination was then calculated as the proportion of the lunar disc illuminated multiplied by the proportion of the night the moon spent above the horizon. Site elevation was extracted from the [Open-Meteo Elevation API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/elevation-api). Distance to clutter and percent clutter were recorded by grid leaders at deployment, and distance to water and water body type were derived from the [BC Freshwater Atlas](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/data/geographic-data-services/topographic-data/freshwater).\
\
For the dynamic occupancy models, we explored additional factors that might influence colonization and extinction: distance to the nearest road and distance to the nearest timber harvest, each measured from the survey location to the closest feature. Road features came from the Human Footprint Index (HFI) layer under development by the Geospatial Centre at Biodiversity Pathways (unpublished data). Harvest features came from the Province of British Columbia's [consolidated cutblocks layer.](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=2e27a5d899fc4c33a32037d392c00767#overview) All continuous covariates were standardized by centering on the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. Missing values were imputed with the global mean before standardization.

Since 2022, insect activity has also been sampled along transect routes using vehicle-mounted sticky traps. Samples are identified to order, and we will evaluate insect abundance as a potential covariate of bat activity in future years.

## Acoustic Processing

In 2025 acoustic analysis mostly followed the standards set in previous years [@rae2022North; @rae2024North]. This included running all files through two automatic classifiers, Kaleidoscope's Bats of North America 5.4.0 classifier and Sonobat 3.0's Northwestern British Columbia classifier, to remove files that do not contain bat pulses and giving a preliminary bat species identification.

Manual vetting largely follows the protocol of @reichert2018 and previous analysis standards developed by WCSC [@rae2022North] . The key difference in the 2024 and 2025 acoustic analysis compared to previous years is that not all automatic species identifications were manually verified. Instead, based on findings from @stratton2022Coupling , at least 50% of recordings were selected for manual verification.

### Subsetting for manual verification

Starting in 2024, the NNW Bat Hub implemented manual vetting of only a subset of all the bioacoustic data collected under the NABat program. Given the project's large scale, manually vetting all recordings is not feasible long-term. To address this, the NNW Bat Hub, in collaboration with WCSC and contractor Brian Paterson, developed procedures to ensure that selecting a subset of recordings for manual review minimizes biases in analytical results. These standards prioritize the accurate identification of rare and difficult-to-recognize species to maintain the integrity of models and analyses.

To ensure data accuracy, manual verification was conducted based on the number of tagged recordings at each site. For sites with 200 or fewer tagged recordings, all non-noise recordings were manually reviewed. For sites with more than 200 tagged recordings, verification depended on the proportion of recordings assigned a species label. All tags for rare species (comprising ≤10% of prior years' identifications) and commonly misidentified species were fully vetted. Specifically, all Eastern Red Bat (*Lasiurus borealis*) tags were manually reviewed due to frequent misclassification as Little Brown Bats (*Myotis lucifugus*). Additionally, recordings of common species were randomly selected for verification until 50% of total recordings were reviewed. If fewer than 50% of recordings had species tags, all classifier-assigned tags were manually verified, and "NoID" recordings were randomly selected until 50% of all recordings were reviewed.

## Statistical Analyses

### Stationary Activity Trends

Stationary activity trends followed closely what was established by WCSC and Dr. Carl Schwarz in 2021 [@rae2022North]. This included conducting trend analyses examining activity patterns in the data collected to date using negative binomial GLMM models with a set of species-specific covariates (@tbl-cov). Species-specific covariates for stationary models were selected using AIC-based stepwise selection (@tbl-cov).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: true
#| label: tbl-cov
#| tbl-cap: "Top-performing stationary models selected by AIC-based stepwise selection. Definitions of covariates are: Temperature = nightly temperature (°C); Wind speed = nightly mean wind speed (km/h); RH = nightly mean relative humidity (%); dd = cumulative degree days above 10 °C since January 1; Moon = proportion of the moon illuminated × proportion of the night the moon was above the horizon; Clutter = distance (m) to the nearest clutter object; Nearby water = whether the detector was within 100 m of water (1 = yes, 0 = no); I(YearS²) = quadratic year term allowing for non-linear temporal trends. A * B denotes the main effects of A and B plus their interaction." 
#| fig.pos: 'H'

kable(model_covariates,
      col.names = c("Species", "Species Code", "Top Performing Model Covariates"),
      label = "model-covariates") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE,
                position = "left") %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "15em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "8em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "20em")
```

All models followed the same basic structure, modelling the total number of detected calls as a negative binomial response with log link:

``` r
Total detections ~ YearS + log(Sample Nights) + (1|Grid Cell ID/Quadrant) 
+ species specific covariates
```

Where total detections is the total number of detected calls of a given species at a site in a given year. YearS is the standardized survey year (years since 2016) and provides the estimate of the temporal activity trend. log(Sample Nights) is the natural logarithm of the number of detector-nights and accounts for variation in sampling effort among site-years. The random intercept (1\|Grid Cell ID/Quadrant) gives one random intercept per cell, plus one per specific quadrant within a cell. This allow baseline activity to vary among grid cells and the quadrants within them.

Model fit was assessed for each final model using simulation-based scaled residuals from the DHARMa package, with 1,000 simulations per model. For each model, we inspected residual quantile–quantile plots and plots of residuals against predicted values and against each predictor. Because large sample sizes can make trivial deviations statistically significant, we evaluated the magnitude of each deviation alongside its p-value to determine good model fit[@harrison2018].

We conducted our statistical analyses at provincial and regional scales. For the regional analyses, we assigned all sampled grid cells to four geographic regions (Southwestern, Southcentral, Southeastern and Northern), each roughly corresponding to a different species set (@fig-map).

#### Use of Automated Identification Results in Stationary Trend Analyses

Stationary trend analyses used AutoID classifications from Kaleidoscope Pro. Manual verification was applied only to flag non-bat noise; where manual review suggested a different species than the AutoID label, the original AutoID classification was retained.

This approach was first identified as necessary in 2023 [@rae2022North], when analyses of manually verified data revealed a consistent positive trend across all species, this was interpreted as an artifact of reviewer learning over time rather than a true biological signal. As verifier experience increased across years, calls were increasingly assigned to specific species rather than left unidentified, producing an apparent increase in detections independent of actual bat activity. Because this observer effect is difficult to control for statistically, AutoID classifications are now used as the standard for all activity trend analyses, as automated classifiers apply consistent criteria across all years. While AutoID is subject to some misclassification, the error rate is consistent across years and does not confound detection of genuine temporal trends.

### Transect Models

The province-wide transect abundance trend models used only completly manually verified detections. Transects are surveyed from a moving vehicle, so each bat is likely recorded only once as the vehicle passes. Call counts therefore serve as an index of relative abundance rather than of activity. When a detection was identified as a species couplet, it was counted toward each species in the couplet.

All models had the same basic structure: total detections were modelled as a negative binomial response with a log link:

``` r
Total detections ~ YearS + log(transect length) + (1|Grid Cell ID) 
+ species specific covariates
```

Total detections is the number of calls of a given species detected on a transect in a given year. YearS is survey year expressed as years since 2016, and provides the estimate of the temporal activity trend. log(transect length) is the natural logarithm of the total length of the transect sampled and accounts for variation in sampling effort among transects. The random intercept (1\|Grid Cell ID) allow baseline activity to vary among grid cells.

Covariates were limited to weather variables, because landscape-level covariates cannot be represented meaningfully for a survey that moves through the landscape. Species-specific covariates for transect models were selected based on those previously established in @rae2022North and were selected using AIC-based stepwise selection (@tbl-cov-transects).

Since transects are only conducted in roughly 50% of our grid cells on a typical year and each transect records fewer bats per night than stationary monitoring, we have elected not to conduct regional-scale transect trend analyses due to low sample sizes.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| include: true
#| label: tbl-cov-transects
#| tbl-cap: "Top-performing transect models selected by AIC-based stepwise selection. Definitions of covariates are: Temperature = nightly temperature (°C); Wind speed = nightly mean wind speed (km/h); RH = nightly mean relative humidity (%); Moon = proportion of the moon illuminated × proportion of the night the moon was above the horizon." 
#| fig.pos: 'H'

kable(transect_covariates,
      col.names = c("Species", "Species Code", "Top Performing Model Covariates"),
      label = "model-covariates") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE,
                position = "left") %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "15em") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "8em") %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "20em")
```

### Dynamic Occupancy

We fitted multi-season (dynamic) occupancy models [@mackenzie2003] to estimate trends in occupancy, colonization, and persistence while accounting for imperfect detection. This analysis used nightly acoustic detection/non-detection data from passive bat detectors deployed at all the sites in British Columbia (BC).

Initial occupancy ($\psi$) was modeled as a function of distance to water and elevation. Colonization ($\gamma$) and persistence ($\varphi$) were modeled as a function of distance to water, elevation, year-varying distance to harvest, and distance to road. Detection probability (p) was modeled as a function of percent clutter, nightly mean temperature, and Julian night. 

We excluded 2016 because few sites were surveyed that year. Starting the time series in 2016 would have required the model to estimate initial occupancy (ψ₁) for the many sites not yet sampled, and a poorly informed ψ₁ can propagate through the colonization and extinction estimates and produce false trends.

To reduce temporal autocorrelation between consecutive nights, we subsampled every other night, using a maximum of four nights per site-year as repeat surveys. Sites were included if they had at least two nights of data in a given year and data from at least two years. After filtering, 185 sites in 63 grid cells in British Columbia were retained. Models were fit separately for each of the 15 bat species.

Models were fit in a Bayesian framework using JAGS (Version 4.3.2) via the jagsUI package (Version 1.6.3) in r (Version 4.5.1). We ran 3 chains in parallel for 30,000 iterations each, discarding the first 15,000 as burn-in and thinning the remainder by 10, yielding 9,000 posterior samples for inference. Priors on all regression coefficients were normal with mean 0 and precision 0.368 (equivalent to a standard deviation of approximately 1.65), and the standard deviation of the region-level random effect was assigned a Uniform(0, 5) prior. Convergence was assessed using Rhat diagnostics, with values below 1.1 taken to indicate convergence. Results are summarized using posterior means and 95% Bayesian credible intervals. We calculated an overall occupancy trend metric (𝜆) as the ratio of estimated occupancy in the final year to that in the initial year; values of 𝜆 \> 1 with 95% credible intervals entirely above 1 indicate an increase in occupancy, values 𝜆\<1 with intervals entirely below 1 indicate a decline, and intervals overlapping 1 indicate an uncertain or stable.

# Results

2025 marked the tenth year of coordinated NABat sampling done in BC. A total of `r SampledGrids2025` grid cells were sampled with the support of over 60 individuals including contractors, volunteers and staff members from BC Parks, BC WLRS, and BC Ministry of Forests. Grid leaders have also collected a total of 16 transect insect sticky trap samples in 2025, which will be added to previous years of data to explore the addition of insect abundance as a covariate in the transect models.

## Species Detection

All 15 species monitored by the program were detected in 2025. Total acoustic activity varied substantially among grid cells and regions (@fig-map). Little brown myotis and silver-haired bat remain two of the most widespread species in the province. Notable changes in 2025 include:

- **Pallid bat** was detected at only one site, in each of 2023 and 2024. In 2025 it was detected at 14 sites across 6 grid cells, its highest site count since monitoring began and slightly above 2022 (13 sites across 6 grid cells). Pallid bat was first recorded in the Kootenay Region in 2022 and was not detected there in 2023 or 2024. In 2025 it was detected at 8 Kootenay sites across 4 grid cells. Two of these grid cells (111466 and 243562) had no previous detections.

- **Eastern red bat** was detected at 35 sites across 17 grid cells in 2025. That is its highest site count to date, although it was found in more grid cells in 2022 (21). Four grid cells had no previous detections: 111466 and 243562 (Kootenay), 194666 (Okanagan) and 186330 (Northern). Eastern red bat was not detected in the South Coastal Region in 2025 after being recorded there each year from 2021 to 2024.

- **Northern myotis** was detected at 15 sites across 10 grid cells in 2025. In the southern Kootenay Region it was detected for the first time at 4 sites across 3 grid cells (20330, 89962 and 218282), near the southern edge of its range.

- **Long-legged myotis** was detected at 76 sites across 39 grid cells in 2025, down from 92 sites across 45 grid cells in 2023 (the highest year of detection for the species). Most of these losses were in the Okanagan Region (8 sites, 5 grid cells) and the South Coastal Region (5 sites, 2 grid cells). The remaining losses were in the Kootenay and Northern regions (3 sites and 1 grid cell each).

@fig-map is an interactive map. Readers can zoom in to see the individual stationary monitoring sites (blue circles), and click a site to open a pop-up with a summary pie chart of total detections by species and year. Readers can also search for specific grid cells using the ![](images/clipboard-4082158342.png){width="26" height="27"} icon.

## Activity and Abundance Trend Models

2025 was the first year in which provincial-scale trends in stationary acoustic activity could be modelled for all 15 bat species. Model diagnostics indicated that all provincial stationary models fit adequately for interpreting the direction of activity trends, although several had minor deviations occurred across most models. Because some assumptions were not fully met, the magnitude of the estimated trends should be interpreted with caution, and we focus on trend direction throughout. For mobile transects, low numbers of recordings limited reliable trend estimation to 8 of the 15 species.\

```{r}
} else {
  regions_top    <- c("Kootenay Region", "Northern Region")
  regions_bottom <- c("Okanagan Region", "South Coastal Region")
  
  make_gt_subtable <- function(data, region_group) {
    cols <- c("Species", paste0(rep(region_group, each = 2), c("_trend_ci", "_p_val")))
    sub_data <- data %>% select(all_of(cols))
    
    # Rename columns to simple names for gt
    new_names <- c("Species", paste0(rep(seq_along(region_group), each = 2), 
                                     c("_est", "_p")))
    names(sub_data) <- new_names
    
    tbl <- gt(sub_data) %>%
      fmt_passthrough(everything()) %>%
      fmt(columns = everything(),
          fns = function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", x))
    
    # Add spanner headers for each region
    for (i in seq_along(region_group)) {
      tbl <- tbl %>%
        tab_spanner(
          label = region_group[i],
          columns = c(paste0(i, "_est"), paste0(i, "_p"))
        )
    }
    
    # Rename columns to display names
    rename_list <- list("Species" = "Species")
    for (i in seq_along(region_group)) {
      rename_list[[paste0(i, "_est")]] <- "Estimate ± 95%CI"
      rename_list[[paste0(i, "_p")]]   <- "P-value"
    }
    tbl <- tbl %>%
      cols_label(.list = rename_list) %>%
      cols_width(
        Species ~ px(130),
        ends_with("_est") ~ px(110),
        ends_with("_p")   ~ px(60)
      ) %>%
      cols_align(
        align = "center",
        columns = ends_with(c("_est", "_p"))
      ) %>%
      tab_options(
        table.font.size = px(14),
        data_row.padding = px(2)
      )
    
    return(tbl)
  }
  
  tbl_top    <- make_gt_subtable(final_table, regions_top)
  tbl_bottom <- make_gt_subtable(final_table, regions_bottom)
  
  knit_print(tbl_top)
}
```

## Dynamic Occupancy Models

We assessed occupancy trends in two ways: the mean yearly change in occupancy across 2017–2025, and the posterior probability that occupancy in 2025 was higher than in 2017. We considered a posterior probability above 0.95 to be strong evidence of an increase, and one below 0.05 to be strong evidence of a decline.

Overall, occupancy increased across British Columbia between 2017 and 2025 for four of the 15 species modelled (@fig-sppocc). Western long-eared Myotis, little brown Myotis, northern Myotis and silver-haired bat all showed a positive mean yearly trend and a high posterior probability of an increase in occupancy from 2017 to 2025, indicating strong evidence of an overall increase. Fringed Myotis was the only species with a consistent decrease in occupancy: its mean yearly change was negative, and the posterior probability that 2025 occupancy exceeded 2017 occupancy was very low, indicating strong evidence of a decline.

Yuma Myotis, western small-footed Myotis, spotted bat, pallid bat and hoary bat showed no detectable occupancy trend. Their mean yearly change was not significant, and the posterior probability of an increase from 2017 to 2025 gave no clear evidence of either an increase or a decline.

Big brown bat showed no significant mean yearly change, but the posterior probability of an increase between 2017 and 2025 was low, which points to a decline over that period. This was driven by a high posterior mean occupancy in the first year and a slightly below-average posterior mean in the last year ([Appendix A: Big brown bat]), so it more likely reflects a stable population with an unusually high starting point than a true decline.

Eastern red bat, long-legged Myotis, Townsend’s big-eared bat and California Myotis had positive mean yearly trends. However, the posterior probability that occupancy was higher in 2025 than in 2017 was not high enough to conclude that occupancy increased overall. This pattern reflects nonlinear change across years (see species specific results in [Appendix A]). Occupancy fluctuated enough to produce a positive mean yearly trend, but the net difference between the first and last years was small, suggesting these species remained relatively stable over the monitoring period.

![Estimated occupancy trends for 15 bat species in British Columbia (2017--2025) fit across all monitoring sites. Points and bars show the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of the linear change in occupancy per year. The dashed line marks zero, where there is no change in mean yearly opccupancy. Colour shows the posterior probability (at ≥ 0.95) that the occupancy in 2025 was higher (green) or lower (red) than in 2017 . Grey means the probability is uncertain. Slope and colour can disagree when trends are non-linear.](Figures/DOccupancy/figB_bc_trends_all_species.png){#fig-sppocc}

Among the regional models, the Kootenay Region showed the most positive trends ( @fig-regocc). Eastern red bat, silver-haired bat, western small-footed Myotis, western long-eared Myotis, little brown Myotis and long-legged Myotis all had a positive mean yearly trend and a high posterior probability of an increase in occupancy from 2017 to 2025.

In the Northern Region, big brown bat had a negative mean yearly trend and a low posterior probability of an increase, indicating a decline. Eastern red bat also had a low posterior probability of an increase, although its mean yearly change was not significant.

In the Okanagan Region, Townsend’s big-eared bat and eastern red bat had positive mean yearly trends and high posterior probabilities of an increase. Fringed Myotis declined, with both a negative mean yearly trend and a low posterior probability of an increase. Yuma Myotis also had a low posterior probability of an increase, although its mean yearly change was not significant.

In the South Coastal Region, hoary bat had a negative mean yearly trend and a low posterior probability of an increase. Silver-haired bat, California Myotis, western long-eared Myotis and Yuma Myotis had positive mean yearly trends and high posterior probabilities of an increase.

![Regional estimated occupancy trends for 15 bat species in British Columbia (2017--2025). Points and bars show the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of the linear change in occupancy per year. The dashed line marks zero, where there is no change in mean yearly occupancy. Colour shows the posterior probability (at ≥ 0.95) that the occupancy in 2025 was higher (green) or lower (red) than in 2017 . Grey means the probability is uncertain. Slope and colour can disagree when trends are non-linear.](Figures/DOccupancy/figC_regional_trends_all_species.png){#fig-regocc}

To show how occupancy varied across space and time, we mapped the model-estimated probability of occupancy at each site for every year from 2017 to 2025 (@fig-occ-slider). The map lets readers select a species and move through the years to see where occupancy has changed. Each point’s colour shows the model’s estimate of for yearly probability of occupancy, while its shape shows whether the species was detected that year (circle) or not (triangle). Because the occupancy model accounts for imperfect detection, a site where a species was not detected can still have a high estimated probability of occupancy. This is especially likely for species that are hard to detect acoustically, or at sites with few survey nights in a given year. The map therefore shows where a species was likely present, not just where it was recorded.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Probability of occupancy per site by year for 15 bat species in British Columbia with reliable occupancy estimates. Use the buttons to switch species and the slider to change year. Circles = detected; triangles = not detected that year; colour = model inference for probability of occupancy."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-height: 8 

sp_list <- c(
  ANPA  = "Pallid bat",
  COTO = "Townsend's big-eared bat",
  EPFU = "Big brown bat",
  EUMA = "Spotted bat",
  LABO = "Eastern red bat",
  LACI = "Hoary bat",
  LANO = "Silver-haired bat",
  MYCA = "California myotis",
  MYCI = "Western small-footed Myotis",
  MYEV = "Long-eared Myotis", 
  MYLU = "Little brown Myotis",
  MYSE = "Northern Myotis",
  MYTH = "Fringed Myotis",
  MYVO = "Long-legged Myotis",
  MYYU = "Yuma Myotis"
)

if (knitr::pandoc_to("html")) {
  make_occ_species_map(sp_list)
}
```

Because the dynamic occupancy model estimates detection probability separately for each year, it also shows how detectability changed over the monitoring period for each species. This lets us account for changes in sampling and processing, such as the equipment change in 2025, so that shifts in detectability are not mistaken for changes in occupancy. The species-specific results ([Appendix A]) show that the probability of detecting pallid bat and eastern red bat increased in 2025, whereas detection probability for all other species stayed within its normal year-to-year variation.

## Challenges and Lessons Learned

#### **Timing of Data Retrieval and Submission**

Field crews across British Columbia continue to reliably collect recordings for their grid cells. However, organizing and submitting these recordings, along with associated metadata, remains a challenge. Delays in data submission from grid leaders extend processing and analysis times, making it difficult to complete reports by the end of the fiscal year. The transition in project management this year further complicated data submission. We anticipate these challenges will be resolved in future years as teams adjust to the new process. To improve efficiency, we plan to increase reminders to grid leaders and provide additional support to address ongoing challenges in data organization and submission.

## Looking Forward

The BC NABat program has yielded a large and robust acoustic dataset that provides solid baseline information on distribution and relative abundance of 12 of 15 resident BC bat species. The data that has been collected so far are an invaluable reference point for BC's bat distributions and activity that improve with each additional year of monitoring. Key considerations for the future of the program include:

- **Manual Verification Efficiency.** This was the first year that the BC monitoring program reduced the proportion of manual vetting carried out in the recordings to \~50% based on the findings from Stratton et al. (2022). Careful consideration of these results compared to previous years will be considered as a guide for future models and analyses.

- **Transect Sampling.** Transects are a relatively high labour/effort source of data than stationary detectors that require participants to work late into the night. They also often do not collect many recordings of bats in BC relative to the stationary detectors. However, transects are still the only source of reliable estimates of relative abundance. While continuing to support current transect sampling efforts, the NNW Bat Hub will work along side other partners to also explore other methods of creating reliable abundance estimates that are less labour intensive.

- **Adding new grid cells.** Efforts will continue to be made to monitor as many of the same grid cells as possible, as the power of the dataset improves with each additional year. Moreover, looking for new opportunities to add new grid cells especially in under sampled regions of the province can help fill knowledge gaps for species distributions. New cells could also be added within ranges of species that are not widespread but easily monitored using acoustics. For example, Fringed Myotis and Spotted Bats are highly suited to acoustic surveillance, but only occur within a small portion of the grid cells being monitored currently

```{r}
#| label: AppendixB
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| output: asis

# ---- Appendix B: per-site popup content, PDF only ------------------------

if (is_pdf) {
  appx_dir <- "Figures/AppendixB"
  if (!dir.exists(appx_dir)) dir.create(appx_dir, recursive = TRUE)

  redraw_pies <- FALSE   # set TRUE (once) after the data change, then back to FALSE
  max_cols    <- 5       # pies per row before wrapping

  # -- helpers -------------------------------------------------------------
  safe_name <- function(x) gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", x)

  summarise_site <- function(sp) {
    sp %>%
      group_by(year, species) %>%
      summarise(n = sum(n, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
      filter(n > 0)
  }

  # one PNG per site: a pie per year, same colours as the map popups
  plot_site_pies <- function(d, file) {
    yrs <- sort(unique(d$year))
    ny  <- length(yrs)

    tot <- d %>% group_by(year) %>% summarise(t = sum(n), .groups = "drop")
    sp_present <- unique(d$species)
    sp_levels  <- c(intersect(names(sp_colors), sp_present),
                    setdiff(sp_present, names(sp_colors)))
    cols <- ifelse(sp_levels %in% names(sp_colors),
                   sp_colors[sp_levels], "#AAAAAA")
    names(cols) <- sp_levels

    d <- d %>%
      left_join(tot, by = "year") %>%
      mutate(
        year_lab = sprintf("%s\n(n = %s)", year, format(t, big.mark = ",")),
        year_lab = factor(year_lab,
                          levels = unique(year_lab[order(year, decreasing = TRUE)])),
        species  = factor(species, levels = sp_levels)
      )

    p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = 1, y = n, fill = species)) +
      geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
      coord_polar(theta = "y") +
      facet_wrap(~ year_lab, ncol = min(ny, max_cols)) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
      guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = ceiling(length(sp_levels) / 9))) +
      theme_void(base_size = 9) +
      theme(
        legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.key.size = unit(8, "pt"),
        strip.text      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8,
                                       margin = margin(b = 3)),
        plot.margin     = margin(2, 2, 2, 2)
      )

    w <- min(ny, max_cols) * 1.35 + 0.4
    h <- ceiling(ny / max_cols) * 1.55 + 0.6
    ggsave(file, p, width = w, height = h, dpi = 200, bg = "white")
    w
  }

  # species x year count table (markdown pipe table -> LaTeX longtable)
  site_table <- function(d) {
    d %>%
      arrange(year) %>%
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
      mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-species))) %>%
      arrange(desc(Total)) %>%
      rename(Species = species) %>%
      mutate(across(-Species, ~ format(.x, big.mark = ",")))
  }

  # -- appendix body -------------------------------------------------------
  cat("\\clearpage\n\n")
  cat("# Appendix B: Species composition by site {.unnumbered}\n\n")
  cat("Pie charts show the proportion of identified bat passes by species for",
      "each year a site was surveyed (most recent first); totals are given",
      "under each year. Tables give the underlying counts.\n\n")

  sites_appx <- sites_plot %>% arrange(site_name)

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(sites_appx))) {
    site <- sites_appx$site_name[i]
    d    <- summarise_site(sites_appx$sp_data[[i]])
    if (nrow(d) == 0) next

    f  <- file.path(appx_dir, paste0(safe_name(site), ".png"))
    ny <- n_distinct(d$year)
    w  <- if (redraw_pies || !file.exists(f)) plot_site_pies(d, f)
          else min(ny, max_cols) * 1.35 + 0.4

    cat("\\needspace{0.35\\textheight}\n\n")
    cat(sprintf("## %s {.unnumbered .unlisted}\n\n", site))
    cat(sprintf("\\begin{center}\\includegraphics[width=%.2fin]{%s}\\end{center}\n\n",
                min(w, 6.5), f))
    cat(knitr::kable(site_table(d), format = "pipe", align = "l"), sep = "\n")
    cat("\n\n")
  }
}
```
